standard.title: Share drama in informal settings
standard.description: share their drama in informal settings
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can share arts works with audiences and respond to questions about their work (Foundation). They have been developing skills in dramatic play, process drama and simple performance within class contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students share their drama in informal settings, communicating to an audience and reflecting on what the drama made them think or feel.

nodes.label: What the audience should experience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify what they want their audience to think about or feel when watching their drama.
nodes.minimum_width: Student can respond to the question 'What do you want your audience to think about your drama?' with at least one idea.
nodes.typical_width: Students consider their personal responses to drama experiences and think about audience perspective; they can describe what they want the audience to notice or feel; they connect their drama-making decisions to an intended audience effect.
wider: Students consider the difference between what they intended and what the audience actually experienced, using simple reflection after sharing
Students explore how different performance choices (facial expression, movement, voice) might produce different effects on an audience
nodes.hinge_reason: If students have no awareness of the audience — no sense that sharing involves communicating something — the performance event is purely expressive without communicative intent; this distinction is what makes 'sharing drama' different from 'doing drama'.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly prompt audience-awareness before sharing: 'Before we share — what do you want people watching to think or feel?' This question is the hinge-prevention move.

success_criteria: Student names at least one thing they want the audience to think about or feel when watching
Student can connect one performance decision (e.g. 'I used a loud voice because...') to an intended effect

nodes.label: Performing and reflecting
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can perform their drama in an informal setting and reflect on the experience as performer and as audience member.
nodes.minimum_width: Student performs their drama to an audience (even a partner) and responds to at least one reflection question afterwards.
nodes.typical_width: Students retell a familiar story or share a drama through acting in an informal setting; they perform sequences (including frozen images or transitions) to communicate key scenes; they reflect using questions about what they liked, what the drama made them think about, and how they felt making and watching it.
wider: Students perform a drama based on a community story, family experience or exploration of First Nations Australians' connection to place, sharing with their class
Students use digital recording to capture and watch back their performance, noticing what communicated well

response_modes.reason: Performance and reflection integrate all prior skills. Post-performance discussion ('What did you like best? Why? What did this drama make you think about?') scaffolds the reflective habit that builds over the later bands.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The range of drama types students can perform and reflect on is varied — frozen image sequences, Readers' Theatre, dramatic play, cultural stories — and experiencing multiple forms builds richer reflective vocabulary.
success_criteria: Student performs their drama in an informal setting to at least one audience member
Student responds to at least one reflection question about what the drama made them think or feel
Student identifies at least one thing they liked in their own or a peer's drama and says why
